short: From January 1, 2029, nobody may offer, sell or conduct a covered AI audit in California without registering with the Government Operations Agency. AB 1405 builds that registry; SB 813 creates a separate, higher designation for independent verification organizations. Licensed CPAs are deemed to satisfy the conduct and reporting rules by following AICPA attestation standards.
title: California AI Auditor Registration: SB 813 and AB 1405
subtitle: California became the first state to regulate who may audit an AI system. Signed September 9, 2026.
body_html:
California signed two AI auditing bills on September 9, 2026. Together they make California the first state to say who may perform an AI audit and on what terms. Both add new chapters to the Government Code and both are administered by the Government Operations Agency.

The two do different jobs and are often described as one thing. AB 1405, Chapter 178, is a registration regime: a public list of AI auditors with conduct rules attached. SB 813, Chapter 179, is a designation regime: a higher, discretionary status for auditors the agency judges to have demonstrated expertise. An auditor can be registered without being designated.

What AB 1405 requires, and from when

The operative sentence is short. Beginning January 1, 2029, a person shall not offer, sell, or conduct a covered AI audit unless registered with the agency. A covered AI audit is defined as one assessing the internal controls, processes or systems implemented for an AI system or model that are necessary for compliance with state law. The obligation attaches to the audit, not to the auditor's location, so a firm outside California auditing for California compliance is inside the definition.

The agency has until January 1, 2029 to establish the registry, set annual fees not exceeding the reasonable cost of administering the chapter, and publish a misconduct reporting mechanism. Registration itself requires the business name and contact details, a list of the California laws under which the auditor conducts audits, any certifications held, a description of services under 500 words, and a standard operating procedure naming the standards applied. That procedure may be redacted for trade secrets.

The conduct rules are the substance. A registered auditor must maintain independence from the auditee, and specifically may not audit its own work, meaning any system, process or control it materially designed, developed, implemented or operated. An individual may not seek or accept employment with the auditee while working on the audit, and may not be assigned to an audit of a company that employed them in a related role within the previous 12 months. Records must be kept for at least ten years. The registration number must appear on advertising that offers audit services.

Every audit report must state its scope and objectives, its results with the documentation supporting them, remediation measures for each deficiency where appropriate, whether the auditee followed its own internal safety standards, and, notably, the limitations of the audit, including anything in scope that was not assessed and any material gaps in the evidence or access available.

The CPA carve-out

AB 1405 treats licensed accountants differently, in two places. A registered auditor holding a current California Board of Accountancy licence, or authorised under the practice privilege provisions, is deemed to satisfy both the report content requirements and the independence standards, provided the report addresses the required subject matter and the auditor complies with the California Accountancy Act, the AICPA Code of Professional Conduct, and AICPA attestation standards.

Enforcement follows the same split. For most registrants, the agency may investigate, and a violation is grounds for removal from the registry and referral to the Attorney General, after written notice and an opportunity to cure or contest. For a CPA or accounting firm in good standing, the agency notifies the Board of Accountancy instead, and the Board investigates under its own existing authority and reports back.

What SB 813 adds

SB 813 creates the independent verification organization, an AI auditor the agency designates as having demonstrated expertise in assessing the risks an AI system poses and in identifying the metrics and methodologies behind that assessment. The agency has until January 1, 2028 to develop application requirements and the criteria for designation, and to develop procedures for suspending or terminating a designation.

The grounds for losing designation are listed: failure to adhere to appropriate standards, material misrepresentation in an application or audit report, conflicts of interest impairing independence, failure to maintain adequate documentation, conduct calling integrity or competence into question, and lapses in cybersecurity. In building the criteria, the agency is directed to consider existing standards from government agencies, national and international auditing and assurance bodies, standards-setting organisations, and independent experts.

Two dates that are often reported wrongly

The agency's deadline to build each system is not the date the obligation starts. SB 813 gives the agency until January 1, 2028 to establish the designation framework. AB 1405 gives it until January 1, 2029 to stand up the registry, and the prohibition on conducting an unregistered covered audit begins January 1, 2029. Reporting that compresses these into a single 2026 effective date is wrong.

Neither statute creates an audit requirement. They govern who may perform an audit that some other law requires, and AB 1405 says expressly that nothing in it affects the conduct of any audit required under another statute that becomes operative before its own effective dates. It also says registration does not constitute recommendation or endorsement by the State of California, and requires that statement to appear on the registry itself.

Who this reaches

Any organisation that performs AI assessments for third parties against California legal requirements, and any organisation that buys them. A buyer after January 1, 2029 will need to confirm its assessor is registered, since the prohibition falls on offering and conducting the audit. Accounting firms already performing attestation work are the most directly affected existing profession, and also the most accommodated by the statute.
